Solutions 2 and 3 are wrong on the layer-group count, so Solution 1 is the only candidate.

**Layer groups give at most 34 classes.** A layer group $G$ maps to its plane action $\rho: G \to \mathrm{Isom}(\mathbb{R}^2)$. The kernel consists of elements fixing the plane pointwise and acting on the normal direction. That kernel has order at most 2, since a second independent reflection would produce a vertical translation, which a rank-2 layer group cannot contain. So each layer group is either:
- isomorphic to its image $\rho(G)$, a wallpaper group (17 types), or
- $\rho(G)\times\mathbb{Z}_2$ when the horizontal mirror $\sigma_h$ is present, since $\sigma_h$ is central.

That gives at most $17+17=34$ abstract types. Solutions 2 (68) and 3 (63) both exceed this bound, so they are wrong.

**Solution 1's layer count is plausibly exact.** All 17 wallpaper groups occur, and all 17 $W\times\mathbb{Z}_2$ occur (take $W$ acting trivially in the normal direction and add $\sigma_h$). Wallpaper groups are pairwise non-isomorphic by Bieberbach's theorem. The $W\times\mathbb{Z}_2$ types can be separated by simple invariants, for example $\mathbb{Z}_3\times\mathbb{Z}_2$ has a unique involution while $p6$ has infinitely many, and $p2\times\mathbb{Z}_2$ has torsion that $pg\times\mathbb{Z}_2$ lacks. I did not verify every pair exhaustively.

**Rod groups (32) are less certain.** Solution 1's breakdown is internally consistent on the cases I spot-checked. For example, $p4/m$ has $F=\mathbb{Z}_4$ and is $\mathbb{Z}_4\times D_\infty$, and $p4_2/m$ has $F=\mathbb{Z}_2$ and is a non-split amalgam, as the solution says. I could not check the full list of 75 groups, so the 32 is unverified.

Solution 1 is the only one that survives the layer-group bound, so I choose it, with moderate confidence because the rod count is unchecked.

CHOICE: 1
